# 001 · A switch cleanup that keeps the money for declined orders

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✗ Violation: 2 of 36 cases changed** | functional | high | cleanup, behaviour change not intended | [`OrderLifecycle#decide`](../../examples/apps/boxoffice/ticketing-domain/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/boxoffice/ticketing/domain/OrderLifecycle.java) | [B8: Behavioural contracts](../../examples/tools/contracts/README.md) |

> Merging one case into its neighbours makes the code shorter, and it still compiles. But a payment captured for a declined order is no longer refunded. This repo happens to have a model-checking unit test written for exactly this property, which also fails; the contract catches it without anyone having thought to write that test.

## The change

The DECLINED branch looked like a special case of 'payment already recorded', so it was folded into the line below it to remove a comment and a branch.

**Before** ([`OrderLifecycle.java`](../../examples/apps/boxoffice/ticketing-domain/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/boxoffice/ticketing/domain/OrderLifecycle.java), line 35):

```java
case PaymentCaptured captured -> switch (current) {
    case PENDING_PAYMENT ->
        captured.seatsStillHeld()
                ? transition(CONFIRMED, SELL_SEATS)
                : transition(REFUND_PENDING, REQUEST_REFUND);
    // The payment service charges an order at most once, so this is not expected. If it happens anyway,
    // the money must go back.
    case DECLINED -> transition(REFUND_PENDING, REQUEST_REFUND);
    case CONFIRMED, REFUND_PENDING, REFUNDED -> unchanged("payment already recorded");
};
case PaymentDeclined _ -> switch (current) {
    case PENDING_PAYMENT -> transition(DECLINED, RELEASE_SEATS);
    case CONFIRMED, DECLINED, REFUND_PENDING, REFUNDED -> unchanged("payment outcome already recorded");
};
```

**After:**

```java
case PaymentCaptured captured -> switch (current) {
    case PENDING_PAYMENT ->
        captured.seatsStillHeld()
                ? transition(CONFIRMED, SELL_SEATS)
                : transition(REFUND_PENDING, REQUEST_REFUND);
    case CONFIRMED, DECLINED, REFUND_PENDING, REFUNDED -> unchanged("payment already recorded");
};
case PaymentDeclined _ -> switch (current) {
    case PENDING_PAYMENT -> transition(DECLINED, RELEASE_SEATS);
    case CONFIRMED, DECLINED, REFUND_PENDING, REFUNDED -> unchanged("payment outcome already recorded");
};
```

@@ -35,14 +35,11 @@

                     captured.seatsStillHeld()
                             ? transition(CONFIRMED, SELL_SEATS)
                             : transition(REFUND_PENDING, REQUEST_REFUND);

-                case DECLINED -> transition(REFUND_PENDING, REQUEST_REFUND);
-                case CONFIRMED, REFUND_PENDING, REFUNDED -> unchanged("payment already recorded");
+                case CONFIRMED, DECLINED, REFUND_PENDING, REFUNDED -> unchanged("payment already recorded");

## What the verifier found

The behaviour changed for 2 of the 36 possible inputs. Each row is a concrete input that shows the difference:

| Input | The contract says | The code now does |
|---|---|---|
| `decide(DECLINED, PaymentCaptured[seatsStillHeld=false])` | `Transition[next=REFUND_PENDING, effects=[REQUEST_REFUND]]` | `Unchanged[reason="payment already recorded"]` |
| `decide(DECLINED, PaymentCaptured[seatsStillHeld=true])` | `Transition[next=REFUND_PENDING, effects=[REQUEST_REFUND]]` | `Unchanged[reason="payment already recorded"]` |

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

Yes, in this repo: `OrderLifecycleTest.moneyAndSeatsStayConsistentForEveryInputSequence` fails (`:ticketing-domain:test`). That test was written for this property. The contract needed no one to anticipate it.

## Why it matters

A customer whose payment is captured after their order was declined is charged and gets no seats. Normally this cannot happen, because the payment service charges each order once. That is exactly why the branch exists: it is the safety net for a broken assumption, and nothing exercises it day to day. The money would be kept silently, and the first sign would be a chargeback.

## Why the verdict is right

The input domain of decide is finite (6 statuses including null × 6 inputs including null), and the method is proved pure, so the verifier runs all 36 inputs against the bytecode. Exactly the 2 inputs where a DECLINED order receives PaymentCaptured changed outcome, and those 2 inputs are the counterexamples. No test had to anticipate them.

## What to do

Revert the merge. If this is truly unreachable, prove it: the system tests' invariant that every payment belongs to a confirmed or refunded order is the property to strengthen, not the safety net to remove.

## Evidence

The proof trusted these JDK APIs to be pure: `java.lang.Enum.ordinal`, `java.lang.MatchException.<init>`, `java.lang.Record.<init>`, `java.lang.runtime.SwitchBootstraps.typeSwitch`, `java.util.List.copyOf`, `java.util.List.of`, `java.util.Objects.requireNonNull`.
